label: text
text: AWAITING DEVELOPMENTS.

label: text
text: He would be a bold man even at this time of day who would profess to foretell the date of the strike with accuracy. In this respect the strike is remarkable. That is because of the fact, as His Excellency the Governor explained in his speech in the Legislative Council on Thursday, that there are no issues to be settled either by compromise or by agreement. There is not a single point on which the contending parties—the strikers and the employers—can possibly hinge on a excuse for a round table conference. In this respect the strike is unique among strikes the world over.

label: text
text: question of how long it will take the strikers to come to their senses and decide that a steady billet in Hongkong is, after all, much preferable to what the Governor neatly termed the "hospitality of Canton." Judging from reports filtering through from that hotbed of intrigue, whilst many may be willing to throw up the sponge the leaders of the movement directed against law and order are bent on prolonging their absence from Hongkong as long as possible. If threats and intimidation have played some part in inducing employees to leave their work here, it is quite certain that these mental instruments of torture exist to a far greater extent in Canton. It is true that some have been permitted to return, but the credentials of these should, if at all possible, be carefully examined.

label: text

label: text

label: text
text: Meanwhile, until “something happens” in Canton, it seems useless to think of the strike here coming to an end so quickly as some would like. All that can be usefully done is to continue with the good work in the absence of the strikers, always remembering, as His Excellency the Governor also did well to point out, that the inconveniences are not all on one side. In fact, the lot of the strikers in Canton may not be altogether an enviable one even when that “something” does happen. Many may find that working peacefully in Hongkong under the protection of the British flag is a thousand times to be preferred to being utilised as “gun fodder” for the rival.

label: text
text: Referred to by the Colonial Secretary during yesterday's Finance Committee meeting was a matter which was overshadowed by the Governor's strike statement but which has a considerable bearing on the future well-being of the community and the efficiency of a very vital service, namely the commencement of wireless communication between Hongkong and the Pratas Shoal. This statement may not to the lay mind appear of sufficient importance to warrant its being bracketed with a matter of such moment as the strike but the initiated see in it something which will endure long when the strike is but a memory, the commencement of a service which, if adequately maintained, will be a most important safeguard not only to Hongkong but to the shipping trade on the welfare of which Hongkong depends for its prosperity. It is, of course, but a commencement and the present typhoon season may be over before regular notifications of typhoon movements, which alone would be of any material assistance, are made available; but it serves to show that the undertaking given by the Chinese Admiralty was not an empty promise although the project has taken long enough to materialise. It was in 1909 that the Chinese Government first agreed to erect such a station although in justice to them it should be stated that definite instructions had been given, which were interfered with by the Revolution in China and that the Great War was also responsible for attention being distracted from the scheme. The Hongkong General Chamber of Commerce has all along interested itself in the matter and the Chinese Maritime Customs, under the Chinese Admiralty, has more or less made itself responsible for the work. It only remains now for the Chinese Government to see to it that an efficient staff is sent to operate the wireless and meteorological station and doubtless the Hongkong Government will do its part in the matter of despatching of provisions and reliefs—the special tug which was to be for this purpose is well on the way to completion.

label: paragraph_title
text: A THOUGHT FOR SUNDAY.

label: text
text: "If thy brother shall trespass against thee-"

label: text
text: The charge not infrequently brought against Christianity—that it is a religion which fails to touch so many practical everyday human needs—generally comes from the man who never reads his Bible. The truth, as all who have made any first-hand study of the Scriptures know, is that one can hardly find a word in the Gospel-record of the sayings of Jesus that is not applicable, and often startlingly so, to some special difficulty or tendency of modern life.

label: text
text: As a case in point: when Christ said, "If thy brother shall trespass against thee, go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone," He might well have been speaking rather to 20th century society of all ranks than to the simple folk of His own time.

label: text
text: We have, or think we have, something against a man. But instead of going to him privately and taxing him with it in frank and friendly guise, as Christ says we should do, we just hold aloof from him "for peace sake," nevertheless seldom failing to open our minds pretty freely on the matter to mutual friends. Such a onesided silence is dross, not gold; and the result is nearly always the setting-up of that most un-christian of human relationships, enmity overlaid by a veneer of politeness. Our forbearance has brought not peace, but a sword.

label: text
text: By a majority of two votes—and the narrowness of the margin was the one hopeful sign in the proceedings—the House of Lords refused a second reading to Lord Astor's Bill to enable peeresses in their own right to sit in the Upper Chamber, remarks the "Sunday Times." By their action they did a grave injustice to the peeresses, the force and logic of whose case have lost nothing by temporary defeat; but they did a worse injustice to themselves. The debuts brought out the least engaging qualities of the Second Chamber, and afforded instances of those very attributes which its detractors are quick to seize upon as examples of the evils of an hereditary House. If the enemies of the House of Lords wanted an argument against that assembly, here was one placed gratuitously in their hands by just those persons presumably most jealous of its good name. Without a doubt, by the rejection of this Bill their lordships lost a great opportunity. They had a chance to refute their critics, and they preferred (if only by a tiny majority) the way of reaction. The result cannot fail to be damaging to their prestige.

To argue in this wise is like arguing that because King John did not broadenst Magna Charta it is unprofitsible to permit broadcasting to-day. But we need not labour the obvious. "Here I be and here I intends to stay" is not a case that requires elaborate refutation.

label: text
text: As for the legal objections raised, they could easily be overcome, as Lord Hewitt made clear in an article of which the Duke of Atholl reminded their lordships. This is not a question of legality, but of justice and expediency, and against these twin arguments the opposition were hard put to it to make out a convincing case. The most formidable, if not the newest, weapon in their armoury was the argument of procrastination: the House of Lords is soon to be reformed; why, not, then, in the interests of compactness, delay the smaller measure till it can be incorporated in the larger. We are bound to say that this argument strikes us as having about it more than a savour of opportunism. But in any case we have yet to learn by what law of right or reason it must be considered improper to do to day what it will, admittedly, be proper to do tomorrow. It is from such defences as these that the peeresses and their sympathisers have for the moment fallen back frustrated. But only for the moment. Into all other departments of public life, women have won their way, and only by two votes did they fail of their last objective. The battle is as surely won as if the Bill had been read a second time.
